item.title: Proton acceleration at interplanetary shocks: A numerical study for the HENON mission
item.description: arXiv:2610.26212v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ESA-ASI HENON CubeSat mission will operate in a distant retrograde orbit about 0.08 au upstream of Earth to provide advance space-weather monitoring. Its instruments include an energetic particle detector measuring protons from 2 MeV to hundreds of MeV. Early detection of energetic particles is crucial for protecting technological infrastructure. To investigate proton acceleration at interplanetary shocks, we developed a test-particle numerical simulation in which protons move in the drift approximation around a parallel shock transition and gain energy through a first-order Fermi process at each crossing. They can propagate around the shock either diffusively or superdiffusively; particle transport affects shock acceleration. Protons were injected at the shock with an energy distribution of about 10 keV and scattered in pitch angle by a collision operator. We varied the pitch-angle scattering time, upstream and downstream plasma speeds, and the type of transport. In the superdiffusive case, a power-law distribution of scattering times was generated by mimicking a L\'evy walk. Multiple runs identify the parameter ranges that yield efficient acceleration and higher energies. For typical parameters, superdiffusive acceleration turns out to be somewhat faster than normal diffusive acceleration. We find that the main control parameter appears to be the upstream shock speed, and that energies in the range of 2-10 MeV can be reached for upstream speeds in the shock frame, $V_1$, of the order of 300 km/s or more. Conversely, for a speed of $V_1 \leq 150$ km/s the proton energy reaches only a few hundred keV. These results help explain why many interplanetary shocks accelerate ions only to moderate energies. They also suggest that when the HENON particle instrument is able to detect energetic protons above 2 MeV, the shock speed in the spacecraft frame is of the order of 800 km/s or more.
item.dc:creator: Luisa Scarivaglione, Giuseppe Prete, Silvia Perri, Gaetano Zimbardo

item.title: Intermittent turbulence as the driver of stochastic heating in the near-Sun solar wind
item.description: arXiv:2610.24296v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding the mechanism by which the energy is dissipated at small scales to heat the outer corona and expanding solar wind, is a primary goal of the Parker Solar Probe (PSP) mission, and an outstanding question in heliophysics. Recent observational case studies have suggested that the dominant dissipation mechanism(s), stochastic heating (SH) or resonant heating (RH), may be modulated by the Alfv\'en `surface' ($M_A = 1$), while theoretical and simulation works predict that the mechanism should be modulated by the level of turbulence imbalance. We measure the local energy transfer (LET) rate from $9.8$ to $55$ solar radii from PSP observations, showing that the LET rate peaks at $M_A \sim 0.4 - 0.9$. We connect enhanced LET rates to signatures of intermittency, highlighting the key role that intermittent fluctuations play in heating the near-Sun solar wind. We compare the LET rate with estimates of the SH rate, finding that below $\sim 15$ solar radii the SH heating rate matches the LET rate provided intermittency is accounted for, regardless of $M_A$, while farther from the Sun, SH is unable to account for the observed LET rate. In contrast to predictions by recent theoretical works, this implies that `imbalanced' intermittent stochastic heating may be a viable mechanism to heat highly imbalanced, low-$\beta$ collisionless plasmas, and is likely an important mechanism of dissipation in the outer solar corona and near-Sun solar wind.
item.dc:creator: Tamar Ervin, Trevor A. Bowen, Alfred Mallet, Stuart D. Bale, Kristopher G. Klein, Mihailo Martinovic, Benjamin D. G. Chandran, Philip A. Isenberg, Orlando Romeo, Roberto Livi, Ali Rahmati, Davin Larson

item.title: Self-Oscillating Photonic Frequency Comb for Sub-THz Local Oscillator Generation in Earth Observation Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.26372v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Earth observation missions rely on microwave and sub-terahertz radiometry for retrieving atmospheric parameters such as temperature, humidity, and cloud properties, with the 183- and 229-GHz spectral regions being particularly relevant. Local-oscillator (LO) generation at these frequencies requires low phase noise and high frequency stability while meeting stringent size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints. Conventional architectures employ dielectric resonator oscillators followed by cascaded frequency-multiplication stages, requiring dedicated generation chains for different frequency bands and increasing hardware complexity. Furthermore, frequency multiplication degrades the phase noise of the generated signal. This work proposes and numerically investigates a reconfigurable self-oscillating microwave photonic architecture for LO generation in Earth observation receivers. Cascaded Mach-Zehnder and phase modulation within an optoelectronic feedback loop generate an optical frequency comb with enhanced higher-order components. A combination of optical filters is used to select the required comb line. First, a conventional bandpass filter with a bandwidth of approximately 10 GHz isolates the spectral region containing the desired component, after which a narrowband dual cavity Bragg grating ring resonator (BGRR) with a bandwidth of approximately 3 MHz provides the final line selection. The selected comb line is then combined with an optical reference derived from the same laser and photodetected to generate the desired millimeter-wave or sub-terahertz signal through optical heterodyning. Numerical simulations are presented for 183- and 229-GHz generation, demonstrating the ability of the same underlying architecture to address multiple LO frequencies by tuning the OEO electrical filter to the appropriate oscillation frequency and selecting the corresponding comb order.
item.dc:creator: Dimitrios Kastritsis, Ioannis Stratakis, Stavros Iezekiel

item.title: Prospects for Astrobiology and Technosignature Searches with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time
item.description: arXiv:2606.00574v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: he Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) will repeatedly measure the brightness of billions of astrophysical sources using six colour filters. We test a simple idea: real physical signals tend to appear as coordinated patterns across several measurements, whereas noise does not; we call this behaviour ``coherence''. We illustrate the approach with three LSST-like simulations: (i) five Kuiper Belt Object (KBO) surface/activity states, (ii) 648 exoplanet spectra with an injected vegetation-red-edge-like spectral feature, and (iii) 500 multiband light curves. In idealised simulations, a weakly active KBO is strongly separated from its inactive counterpart when all five colours are combined. The injected red-edge-like feature becomes detectable at effective visible-disc coverage of about 13\%, and stacking about 150 detections could reach 5$\sigma$. Coherent, natural, and noise-like variability occupy distinct regions. A small Gaia DR3 stellar sample illustrates how colour and stability may help prioritise Galactic search regions.
item.dc:creator: Andjelka B Kovacevic, Nigel J. Mason, Aleksandra Ciprijanovic, Becky Long, Dominika Korczakowska, Maia Moore, Juulia Vuolukka
